context.objective: Document how we carry out KYC & Sanctions Screening, the controls and what needs confirmation.

turns.text: To begin with, we open the KYC event and identify the requirements. That is done by: KYC and AML preparer. Before starting we need trigger notice and investor and entity details. What we do: record the trigger: new subscription, ownership change, transfer, subsequent investor close, periodic review, or another trigger event; identify investor type, jurisdiction, structure complexity, regulatory classification, and existing status; determine the approved document and screening requirements for that profile; keep capital acceptance, portal access, and allocation participation blocked until clearance. The check on it: do not provide access or accept capital before documented clearance. Next, we collect and validate identity and entity documentation. That is done by: KYC and AML preparer. Before starting we need list of requirements and investor submissions. What we do: collect subscription agreement, identity records, entity documents, and required supporting data; check legal names, jurisdiction, required addresses and identifiers, and controlling-person information for completeness and consistency; record missing, expired, inconsistent, or unreadable documents and request correction. The check on it: all required documents are complete and internally consistent If something goes wrong: Do not proceed to clearance while required documents are.
How does the preparer learn that one of those trigger events has occurred?

After that, we identify beneficial owners and controlling persons. That is done by: KYC and AML preparer. Before starting we need entity and ownership documents and the approved threshold policy. What we do: map direct and indirect ownership through every entity level; trace ownership through holding companies and intermediate feeder or blocker entities until reaching individuals who meet the approved BO threshold; identify controlling persons even when ownership threshold is not met, as required by policy; compare ownership percentages and relationships, resolve differences, and document any gaps. The check on it: all required ownership levels are traced, and the list of parties to screen is complete. Then, we perform sanctions screening and resolve potential matches. That is done by: KYC and AML preparer; AML reviewer. Before starting we need complete list of parties to screen and verified legal names and aliases. What we do: use Exiger to screen the investor, legal names, aliases, beneficial owners, and controlling persons against approved sanctions and restricted-party sources; keep the search inputs, date, and results; for each potential match, compare identifiers and supporting information to decide whether it is a false positive, a possible match, or a true match; document the resolution and reviewer decision; escalate unresolved or true-match concerns. The check on it: every potential match has documented resolution or active escalation.
What has to be true for the KYC event to be documented as cleared?

Once that is done, we review PEP status and adverse media. That is done by: KYC and AML preparer; AML reviewer. Before starting we need list of parties to screen and approved tools and sources. What we do: screen for PEP status, close associates, and adverse media; under the approved policy, assess each flag's relevance, identity match, recency, and risk; perform EDD when required by a flag; document the findings and the risk that remains after controls (residual risk). The check on it: flags are resolved or escalated before clearance If something goes wrong: EDD requirements and who may approve them are not specified. Following that, we assign risk rating and approval route. That is done by: KYC and AML preparer; AML reviewer. Before starting we need documents, BO, sanctions, PEP, and adverse-media results. What we do: assess jurisdiction, structure complexity, PEP exposure, connections to sanctions risks, and adverse media; apply the approved risk model; record the risk rating, rationale, required approver, and review frequency; send the case to the required reviewer. The check on it: the rating rationale and required approver are documented If something goes wrong: The rating scale, scoring, thresholds, approval matrix, and review-.
How does the risk rating determine the approval route?

Following that, we make and record the AML decision. That is done by: AML reviewer; Compliance Officer for escalations. Before starting we need complete case and risk assessment. What we do: review completeness, screening match resolutions, EDD, the risk rating, and open items; approve clearance only when all required issues are resolved; record the approval, approver, date, conditions, and review requirement; if screening fails or remains prohibited or unresolved, keep the required block in place, escalate to the Compliance Officer, and notify the client as applicable. The check on it: the reviewer signs off; an urgent business need cannot override failed screening. Following that, we apply clearance status and retain the record. That is done by: KYC and AML preparer and the applicable onboarding or operations role. Before starting we need documented AML decision. What we do: communicate the clearance or blocked status to , , , and the applicable payment or event teams; allow capital acceptance, portal access, and allocation participation only after clearance; store the screening, beneficial-ownership, risk, approval, and resolution records under the AML retention policy; record the next review and monitoring requirement. The check on it: the status in operational systems matches the AML decision If something goes wrong: System fields, repository, and retention period require.
What result is this screening process meant to deliver for the investor or the business?

Following that, we perform periodic, trigger, and payment-time monitoring. That is done by: KYC and AML monitoring role; the exact title is not specified. Before starting we need list of active investors, review schedule, trigger alerts, and payment event. What we do: perform the annual or risk-based review under the approved schedule; open a review for changes to a name, entity, ownership, transfer, screening alert, adverse media, or country risk; complete payment-time screening where required by or another checklist; update the risk and clearance status, and communicate any blocks; for European distribution payees blocked by CDD, withhold payment and follow the 30/60/90-day follow-up schedule in . The check on it: do not defer trigger events until the next periodic review If something goes wrong: The monitoring owner, alert source, and review service-level.
Where does this work create the most manual effort or delay in practice?

topics.answer: KYC & Sanctions Screening
The work establishes and communicates an AML clearance or blocked status for an investor event, governing whether capital acceptance, portal access and allocation participation may proceed.

The KYC and AML preparer records a trigger event, which may be a new subscription, ownership change, transfer, subsequent investor close, periodic review, or another trigger event. Trigger notice and investor and entity details are needed before starting.
Monitoring includes annual or risk-based reviews and reviews triggered by changes to names, entities, ownership or transfers, screening alerts, adverse media or country risk. A payment event is an input to payment-time monitoring.
The monitoring alert source and review service level are unspecified.

Clearance requires all required issues to be resolved and reviewer sign-off. Closeout includes communicating the decision, retaining case records, recording the next review and monitoring requirement, and checking that operational-system status matches the AML decision.

The KYC and AML preparer performs the opening and document-collection steps.
The role accountable for the overall KYC and sanctions screening result, distinct from the preparer, is not established.
The monitoring role's exact title and monitoring owner are unspecified.

The KYC and AML preparer opens the KYC event, identifies requirements, and records the trigger. The preparer identifies investor type, jurisdiction, structure complexity, regulatory classification, and existing status, then determines approved document and screening requirements for that profile.
The preparer collects and validates identity and entity documentation, including subscription agreements, identity records, entity documents, and required supporting data. The preparer checks legal names, jurisdiction, required addresses and identifiers, and controlling-person information for completeness and consistency; missing, expired, inconsistent, or unreadable documents are recorded and correction is requested.
After document validation, the KYC and AML preparer uses entity and ownership documents and the approved threshold policy to map direct and indirect ownership through every entity level, including holding companies and intermediate feeders or blockers, to individuals meeting the approved beneficial ownership threshold. The preparer also identifies controlling persons below the threshold as policy requires, compares percentages and relationships, resolves differences and documents gaps.
The KYC and AML preparer and AML reviewer perform sanctions screening using Exiger, a complete list of parties and verified legal names and aliases. They screen the investor, beneficial owners and controlling persons against approved sanctions and restricted-party sources, compare identifiers and supporting information for potential matches, document resolutions and reviewer decisions, and escalate unresolved or true-match concerns.
After sanctions screening, the KYC and AML preparer and AML reviewer screen the listed parties for PEP status, close associates and adverse media using approved tools and sources. Under approved policy they assess each flag's relevance, identity match, recency and risk, perform enhanced due diligence (EDD) when a flag requires it, and document findings and residual risk.
After the PEP and adverse-media review, the preparer and AML reviewer use the documents, beneficial ownership, sanctions, PEP and adverse-media results to assess jurisdiction, structure complexity, PEP exposure, sanctions-risk connections and adverse media. They apply the approved risk model, record the rating, rationale, required approver and review frequency, and send the case to the required reviewer.
With the complete case and risk assessment, the AML reviewer reviews completeness, screening-match resolutions, EDD, the risk rating and open items. The reviewer approves clearance only when all required issues are resolved and records approval, approver, date, conditions and review requirement; the Compliance Officer handles escalations.
If screening fails or remains prohibited or unresolved, the required block remains in place, the case is escalated to the Compliance Officer and the client is notified as applicable.
After a documented AML decision, the KYC and AML preparer and applicable onboarding or operations role communicate clearance or blocked status to applicable payment or event teams, retain the screening, beneficial-ownership, risk, approval and resolution records under the AML retention policy, and record the next review and monitoring requirement.
The KYC and AML monitoring role performs annual or risk-based reviews under the approved schedule, using the active-investor list and review schedule. It opens a review for changes to a name, entity, ownership or transfer, or for a screening alert, adverse media or country risk; it updates risk and clearance status and communicates blocks.
The monitoring role completes payment-time screening where required. For European distribution payees blocked by CDD, payment is withheld and the 30/60/90-day follow-up schedule is followed.

Capital acceptance, portal access, and allocation participation remain blocked until documented clearance. Required documents must be complete and internally consistent; the preparer records missing, expired, inconsistent, or unreadable documents and requests correction, and does not proceed to clearance while required documents are missing.
The repository where screening evidence is retained remains unspecified.
The ownership check requires all required levels to be traced and the list of parties to screen to be complete. Each potential screening match is classified as a false positive, possible match or true match using identifiers and supporting information; every match must have a documented resolution or active escalation.
PEP and adverse-media flags must be resolved or escalated before clearance. The risk-rating check requires the rating rationale and required approver to be documented.
The AML reviewer signs off after reviewing the complete case, including match resolutions, EDD, risk rating and open items. An urgent business need cannot override failed screening; operational-system status is checked against the AML decision.
Trigger events must not be deferred until the next periodic review.

Document and screening requirements are determined for the investor profile, including investor type, jurisdiction, structure complexity, regulatory classification and existing status.
Specific differences in profile-based requirements and any client- or fund-specific routes remain unspecified.
Where ownership passes through holding companies or intermediate feeder or blocker entities, the preparer traces it through those levels to qualifying individuals.
A flag requiring EDD adds enhanced due diligence to the PEP and adverse-media review.
For European distribution payees blocked by CDD, payment is withheld and a 30/60/90-day follow-up schedule applies.

Capital acceptance, portal access and allocation participation are blocked until documented clearance.
Failed, prohibited or unresolved screening keeps the required block in place, triggers escalation to the Compliance Officer and may require client notification.

The described collection includes subscription agreements, identity records, entity documents, and required supporting data; investor submissions are inputs to collection and validation.
Entity and ownership documents and the approved threshold policy are inputs to ownership tracing. Screening retains search inputs, date, results, match resolutions and reviewer decisions.
PEP and adverse-media findings and residual risk are documented. The risk-rating record includes the rating, rationale, required approver and review frequency.
The AML decision record includes approval, approver, date, conditions and review requirement. Screening, beneficial-ownership, risk, approval and resolution records are retained under the AML retention policy.
The active-investor list, review schedule and trigger alerts are inputs to monitoring; the participant also refers to an approved schedule and a 30/60/90-day follow-up schedule.
The repository and retention period for AML records require clarification.

Requirements depend on the investor profile; ownership tracing can extend through holding companies and intermediate feeder or blocker entities.
Whether the route is GPFS-wide or client-specific is not established.

The preparer determines approved document and screening requirements for the investor profile. Required documents must be complete and internally consistent before clearance proceeds.
Documented clearance is a prerequisite to providing access or accepting capital, and clearance is also a prerequisite to allocation participation.
The source and authority for profile-specific requirements and the approved beneficial ownership threshold policy remain unspecified.
The approved beneficial ownership threshold policy governs which individuals are identified by ownership; controlling persons are also identified when the threshold is not met, as required by policy.
The reported approved policy governs flag assessment and whether EDD is required; the approved risk model is applied to assign the risk rating.
EDD requirements and who may approve EDD are unspecified. The rating scale, scoring, thresholds and approval matrix are also unspecified.
Clearance is approved only after all required issues are resolved; an urgent business need cannot override failed screening. Capital acceptance, portal access and allocation participation are allowed only after clearance.
Monitoring follows an approved annual or risk-based schedule. Trigger events must not be deferred to the next periodic review; CDD-blocked European distribution payees follow a 30/60/90-day follow-up schedule with payment withheld.
The source and criteria for required payment-time screening and the document containing the European distribution follow-up schedule are not identified.

The clearance or blocked status is communicated to applicable payment or event teams so the operational activities remain blocked or may proceed after clearance. Other intended recipients were not named in the account.

Exiger is used to screen the investor and relevant parties against approved sanctions and restricted-party sources.
The operational system fields and record repository are unspecified.

topics.answer: The intake calls the work KYC & Sanctions Screening. The reported work covers investor KYC, AML decisions and monitoring; other names and the precise boundary are UNKNOWN.

The work produces an AML clearance or blocked status and controls access, capital acceptance and allocation participation. The participant did not explicitly state the overall intended result or value.

Reported triggers include subscriptions, ownership changes, transfers, subsequent investor closes, periodic reviews and other events. Monitoring is annual or risk-based and also addresses trigger events and payment-time screening where required. European CDD-blocked distributions follow a 30/60/90-day schedule. Notice origin, receiver and other deadlines are UNKNOWN.

The reviewer signs off; status is communicated, records are retained and operational status is checked against the decision. Clearance permits specified activities, while failed or unresolved screening is blocked and escalated. The overall finish, the sequence of status and record activities, and blocked-case resolution are UNKNOWN.
UNKNOWN. Preparers, reviewers, the Compliance Officer and a monitoring role perform reported work, but overall accountability was not identified.

The preparer opens and profiles the event, collects and checks documents, requests correction for defects and traces owners and controllers. The preparer and AML reviewer screen sanctions and PEP/media, assess flags and rate risk; the case is sent to the required reviewer for an AML decision. Status and records are then handled, and periodic, trigger and payment-time monitoring is reported. Correction returns, individual assignments, record locations and monitoring handoffs remain UNKNOWN.

Reported checks cover document consistency, complete ownership tracing, match resolution or escalation, flag resolution or escalation, rating rationale and approver, reviewer sign-off and operational status against the AML decision. Clearance requires all required issues to be resolved; failed screening cannot be overridden for urgency. Evidence locations, segregation, system enforcement, thresholds, failed-check rework and client approval scope are UNKNOWN.

EDD is performed when a flag requires it; payment-time screening is performed where required; European distribution payees blocked by CDD have payments withheld and a 30/60/90-day follow-up. Detailed criteria, sources, effort, charging, removal constraints and boundary comparisons remain UNKNOWN.
UNKNOWN. The participant did not describe manual effort, delays or workarounds.
